contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the First Minister: Weather, wildfires, drought and resilience
contributions.text_english:
I'd like to start by thanking the firefighters, emergency responders, public services, volunteers and local communities affected by the wildfires this summer. While I and my colleagues welcome this statement today, let's be clear, this is far from what the public should expect from a Government. There is no doubt that the wildfires across Wales this summer were a national crisis. Fire and rescue services were pushed to the brink. People were evacuated, homes and farmland destroyed, and large swathes of the country were covered in smoke.

People who were miles away from these fires were impacted by the smoke, and the Government failed to understand the public health concern across the country. It's nearly two months after the first wildfires. The Government will know that those fires were much earlier than we would usually start to see wildfires, and, sadly, they continued across Wales.

As Welsh Labour, we requested that this Senedd should have been recalled for Members to raise questions and for the public to have the opportunity to hear from the Government. In a national crisis, with so much of Wales on fire, I do not believe the Plaid Cymru Government acted quickly and decisively. The lack of information and updates from Government Ministers made it feel like this Government did not grasp the severity of the crisis. The extent of the damage to communities, the economy, the environment and wildlife must not be forgotten because the fires are no longer burning.

I'd like to know what work the Government is undertaking to understand the impact of the wildfires on the Welsh economy in urban and rural areas. The significant pressure on resources arising from the number and complexity of fire incidents was unprecedented. Having been in close contact with the FBU throughout the Senedd recess, they have made it clear to me that the Welsh Government must accept the incidents this summer demonstrated inadequate firefighting resources.

It's also important to highlight the control centre staff, including those at South Wales Fire and Rescue Service, who handled 8,466 calls between 19 July and 1 September. Emergency services worked tirelessly for weeks whilst under relentless pressure. It would be good to know what engagement the Welsh Government has had with relevant unions since July and when the social partnership forum met. 

Further learning will emerge over the coming months, but there are certain aspects that are already evident. I was grateful to you, First Minister, for allowing a briefing with Welsh Government officials during recess. At that briefing on 28 July, I raised the issue of communication. The crisis escalated in the following days, but there appeared to be a lack of continued strategic co-ordination between Government, NRW, local authorities, Public Health Wales, health boards and other partners. It was not communicated effectively or efficiently to the public or Members. There was undoubtedly a public health aspect to the crisis, and I'd like to know what this Government is doing to examine the full extent of this.

With the impact of climate change, extreme weather events are likely to become the norm, not the exception. There is a very real worry that fire and rescue services could find themselves facing a similar crisis situation due to flooding. Preparedness requires leadership and investment at a national level. I welcome the climate and nature action plan. The Welsh Government must work to ensure councils, communities and businesses are as prepared as possible for future significant weather events. This can't fall on individual local authorities. A climate resilience fund is one of the measures suggested for consideration by the FBU. Can the First Minister confirm whether this is something the Government will explore?

Prif Weinidog, I welcome what you have said today, but we need to see outcomes, not just promises. Political leadership is about being present and visible. It's also about learning and listening. I hope the Welsh Government is listening to the communities who watched in terror as flames approached, to the exhausted fire and rescue services, to the farmers whose crops were destroyed, and to the business owners who suffered significant financial losses. Firefighters, communities and businesses need to know that lessons have genuinely been learnt from this unprecedented summer. How will you measure the success of the climate change and reliance summit, and when will the climate and nature action plan be delivered? Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 7. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women's Health: Putting Women, Babies and Families at the Heart of Safety: The implementation of Call for Concern in Maternity and Neonatal Services
contributions.text_english:
I'd like to thank the Deputy Minister for her important statement today. Care provided during pregnancy, birth and the first few weeks of a baby's life is critical for not only the babies and mothers, but also for the well-being of entire families. When women do not receive the care they need and deserve during this time, then the outcome is often very tragic. Call for Concern is an important system to ensure that people's voices are front and centre of their care, and this has a particular importance in maternity and neonatal services. As the Deputy Minister has pointed out, women and families are often the first to identify that something might be wrong.

Of course, Call for Concern only works if the workforce and services are able to act upon it. Last year, the previous Welsh Labour Government commissioned an all-Wales assurance assessment of maternity and neonatal services to assess the safety and quality of services. The voices and experiences of women and families were at the centre of that assessment, as they should be. It is their perspectives that are key to understanding the quality, safety and culture of these services. So, can the Deputy Minister provide an assurance today that the recommendations of 'The path to safer beginnings' report will be fully implemented, supported by clear delivery timelines and transparent reporting?

Alongside identifying areas for essential improvement in maternity and neonatal services in Wales, the report highlighted the dedication and professionalism of the workforce. The Royal College of Midwives has identified workforce capacity as the most pressing challenge currently facing maternity services in Wales. This includes ensuring sufficient opportunities for newly qualified midwives, as well as improving the retention of experienced staff. These pressures will continue to impact the safety, quality and accessibility of care for women and families if action is not taken. Targeted investment in midwifery staffing, alongside improvements in workforce planning and retention, is an intervention that supports both immediate services and longer term sustainability.

Access to perinatal mental health and parent-infant services are vital for mental health and women's health. So, will the Deputy Minister confirm today the delivery and full funding of the perinatal workforce plan? In addition, maternity services also play a central role in supporting wider women's health. Ensuring maternity services are fully integrated into the delivery of the women's health plan will maximise the impact of both workforce investment and service improvement.

The preventative impact of maternity and neonatal services cannot be overstated. In recent decades, they have had to adapt to changing demands of care and shifting demographics. Women in Wales are generally giving birth at older ages, with around 55 per cent aged 30 or over, compared with 42 per cent in 2011. There's also been an increase in the number of pregnant women classed as being obese, as well as having a mental health condition. A strengthened partnership between the NHS, unions, patients and local government will be absolutely critical to meeting the shared challenges ahead. Mothers, babies and families should be in no doubt that they will receive the highest possible standard of maternity and neonatal care regardless of where they live in Wales.

Today, women and babies living in Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board are not receiving visits and support from health visitors because they have been forced to go on strike. I know this comes under the Cabinet Secretary for health, but it's important to mention it here today when we're talking about listening to the concerns of women and families. I once again want to implore the Welsh Government to help resolve this dispute, as Plaid Cymru said they would do in opposition. Without staff, the Call for Concern system cannot work as intended across maternity and neonatal services. Medical interventions during birth have increased rapidly in recent years, and the proportion of caesareans has reached record levels. This increase has changed the demands being placed on maternity services, so I'd like to know what work the Government is doing to examine how services need to be adapted to respond to this changing demand. Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
contributions.text_english: Diolch, Lywydd. Our dedicated staff in our NHS work tirelessly, and in recent weeks many have experienced incredibly challenging working conditions due to the hot weather. Last month, the Welsh Ambulance Services University NHS Trust declared a critical incident following one of the busiest periods of sustained pressure on services in recent years. Demand was well in excess of normal levels as a result of the extreme heat, and I understand there was a noticeable increase in the number of young people presenting with symptoms of dehydration. We're accustomed to the NHS needing to prepare for the winter pressures, but what action is the Government taking to ensure that services, buildings and the workforce are equipped to deal with the impact of hot weather?

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
contributions.text_english:
Diolch and, absolutely, the workforce is absolutely crucial. Earlier today, alongside my colleague Shav Taj, I met student midwives from the September 2023 cohort. They feel as though they've been left in limbo, with no jobs available. One newly-qualified midwife told me she was now working as a water technician, and others are working as baristas and in the hospitality sector. The students have been told that there might be opportunities to work in health and social care, but this is not what they want or that they're qualified to do. Now, I know the Minister is aware of the situation, but the student midwives cannot have been clearer today; they feel left behind and they feel without hope.

Welsh Labour protected the NHS Wales bursary scheme, supporting the next generation of healthcare workers to train and work in the Welsh NHS, but, without clinical experience, student midwives can't get jobs and they can't use their degree for anything else. One option would be to extend the bursary for another year to cover the preceptorship training that enables midwives to transition to professional practice. So, will the Welsh Government consider this as one option?

contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: Improving access to local economic opportunities in Casnewydd Islwyn
contributions.text_english: I thank the Member for bringing this important debate here today. Coleg Gwent is the largest provider of full-time further education in Wales, with over 18,000 learners, including campuses in Newport and Crosskeys, and the college is a major employer, with over 1,200 staff. The college is seeing record levels of applications for courses, and I think everyone in this Senedd would agree that colleges like Coleg Gwent are vital in preventing young people from being lost to long-term disengagement from education and the labour market. They always give people a second chance, and I look forward to seeing how this new Welsh Government will support them. Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the First Minister
contributions.text_english: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. Earlier this year, Premier Forest Products in Newport became the first private sector company to sign the Welsh Government's corporate parenting charter. Working in partnership with Newport City Council, Premier Forest provides paid work placements for care-experienced young people. Opportunities are offered across all departments, helping participants gain practical experience of the workplace and transition into employment. Terry Edgell, chief executive officer of Premier Forest Products, is clear that commercial success comes with social responsibility, and I've seen and heard first-hand what a difference this makes to young people, the company and also the workforce. So, I'd like to know: what is the Welsh Government doing to encourage and support more employers to give opportunities like this to care-experienced young people across Wales?

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
contributions.text_english: Once again, yesterday, trains on the Ebbw Vale line stopping in Newport were cancelled. Transport for Wales said this was due to more trains than usual needing repairs, and this is not the first time that this has happened. I know how disruptive these cancellations are for local people, and this is in addition to frequently overcrowded trains due to the limited number of carriages. People rely on these trains to get to work and college, and delays and cancellations have a big impact. It does seem that every time there is a problem on another part of the network it is this line that is most often hit. This is not fair and has a disproportionate impact on people relying on the Ebbw Vale line. I'd like to hear from the transport Minister how he will ensure a full and regular service on the Ebbw Vale line.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
contributions.text_english:
Thank you to the Deputy Minister for her statement today. As Welsh Labour's spokesperson, I welcome the cross-Government approach to preventative health, but I'm interested in what outcomes will be delivered for people across Wales. You've mentioned today the designated preventative departmental expenditure line within the Welsh budget for 2027-28, but I'm sure you'd agree, Minister, that it isn't just the creation of the budget line itself that we should be focused on, but rather how people's overall health and well-being will improve. I, like many others, challenge the Government to go beyond the process. We want to know what exactly will change and how success will be measured during this Senedd term.

I'm glad the Deputy Minister mentioned two very effective interventions: screening and vaccinations. It's good to hear the Deputy Minister supports the continuation of the national lung cancer screening programme, which was introduced by the Welsh Labour Government. I'm surprised there's no mention today of the HPV vaccine. Since it was introduced in 2008, the HPV vaccine has reduced cervical cancer rates by almost 90 per cent in women in their 20s, and that has saved hundreds of lives every year across the UK. So, I'd like to know how the Government will engage with schools across Wales to encourage participation in vaccination programmes like this.

Cervical screening also saves lives, and there's work to be done to make that more accessible. So, I'd like to see the Government learn from areas where there have been increases in screening uptake. You did give one example of screening uptake best practice, but I think there have been some other ones, particularly in London, where GPs have adapted to offer appointments for their clinics that fit in with people's work and family lives, such as on weekends and late evenings. So, I'd be interested to hear if you've been able to look into that.

Encouragement to help break down stigma is also key to increasing screening uptake. So, I'd like to know how Public Health Wales is focusing screening delivery that is tailored to local communities, for instance consistent breast screening opportunities in each geographical area throughout the year to support local health board demand. There's also work to be done engaging with businesses and organisations to support their workforce to attend all screening as a priority.

Targeted communications and education are important, breaking down stigma for everyone, but specifically for those attending their first screening appointment. We all know the way people access information is changing, and I'd like to know how national screening programmes are adapting to fit into those communication methods to reflect this.

Inclusion health is a globally recognised approach to address and prevent the health inequalities facing marginalised groups who struggle to access health services and experience far poorer health outcomes. We know that there's a huge human cost to these inequalities, as well as a cost to public services such as blue light services, A&E and emergency inpatient treatment. A stark example is people experiencing homelessness who experience acute physical and mental health problems and die 30 years younger than the general population.

There are some fantastic examples of inclusion health work led by Public Health Wales and services such as Cardiff and Vale inclusion service, and the partnership work between Ysbyty Gwynedd and Cyngor Sir Ynys Môn. However, this is often reliant on passionate individuals going above and beyond the remit of their roles, rather than inclusion health being prioritised, systematic and integrated with health services. Prioritising inclusion health is key to preventative health, as well as delivering significant savings to emergency health services. So, will you commit to making inclusion health one of your ministerial priorities, and consider developing an inclusion health strategy?

Finally, we know that sport helps to tackle obesity and to prevent physical and mental health conditions. Professional and grass-roots sport clubs play a leading role, and their impact is far-reaching. They are trusted places at the heart of our communities. I'd also recommend to you the Fit Fans programme, which works across our football league clubs. In Plaid Cymru's manifesto, you said you would invest in sports and physical activity as part of the preventative health agenda, and you've mentioned today your discussions with the Minister for culture and sport. However, any new work stream does need funding. The health minister couldn't give an answer when I previously asked how much that investment will be and where the money will come from. So, can you, Deputy Minister, today tell us that? Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
contributions.text_english: Diolch. I know it seems to be strange talking about flooding during the summer and on what is one of the hottest days, however, for people who have been flooded or who are at risk of flooding, that concern lasts all year round. The £25 million Stephenson Street scheme in the Lliswerry area of Newport was completed last autumn. It reduced the flood risk from the River Usk to more than 2,000 homes and businesses. Upstream, a tributary of the River Usk at Caerleon, the Afon Lwyd, poses a flood risk to nearby homes and sports clubs. I've met with residents, Natural Resources Wales and sports clubs, and local people are still waiting for clarity from Natural Resources Wales about planned flood defences. The Welsh Labour Government invested record levels of funding for flood defences. So, can the Minister reassure my constituents that this Government will invest in flood defences to protect our communities?

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women's Health: Priorities for social care, mental health and women's health
contributions.text_english:
Thank you to the Minister for the statement today. I'd like to start with a topic that I know many other Members are passionate about, and that's women's health. For far too long, women's voices and experiences in the healthcare system have not been given their due weight. And in the last Senedd, the Welsh Labour Government's women's health plan was a significant step and ensured that there is a focus on women's health in our NHS.

I'm personally proud of what we achieved in Government to put more focus on women's health, from free period products, to menopause support, to creating women's health hubs in every health board. But there is, of course, much more to do, and Plaid Cymru must keep up the momentum. 

It was disappointing to see that there is no dedicated action for women's health in Plaid Cymru's pledges for their first 100 days in Government. We will hold the Government to account to ensure that women across Wales get the care that they deserve, and that the goals of the women's health plan are funded and delivered in full.

I'd specifically like to ask about endometriosis, which, as the Minister will know, affects one in 10 women in Wales and can be truly debilitating. I know from constituents that too many women find themselves being dismissed, with symptoms not taken seriously. And the impact on women's well-being and careers can be absolutely devastating. 

In Government, we had committed to developing accredited regional centres for endometriosis care across Wales, to improve access to specialist support. This was alongside a network of community and primary care endometriosis clinics to be based in the new women's health hubs. I note that the Minister said she's carefully considering the women's health model. I'm just disappointed that you can't commit today to continuing that important work, and I'm really keen that we have clarity as soon as possible.

Advances are being made in diagnosis, and we must make sure we're ready to adapt to these new developments. Rapid endometriosis tests have just been given the go-ahead by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, which will help to significantly reduce the time it takes for women to be told whether they have the condition. One test, I believe, provides that result in 45 minutes. Currently, getting a diagnosis can take years. So, when does the Minister expect women in Wales to be able to access those new tests?

On social care, I was pleased to see the Government's long-term commitment to developing a national care service, and this is an ambition that we share. One of the key opportunities for strengthening our social care system is by improving integration with local authorities. So, what concrete steps will the Minister take to bring these systems closer together and ensure that people receive more seamless care at the time they need it most?

And I'm proud of how the Welsh Labour Government fought to properly reward our social care workforce, including through legally enforced fair pay agreements. And, of course, our social care system across Wales would not work without the huge contribution of unpaid carers—people who look after their loved ones, often in the most difficult of circumstances, to help them live as well as possible. 

Earlier this year, the Welsh Labour Government consulted on a new strategy for unpaid carers, and we need to see progress on this. Minister, you said today that the Government is investing in the short breaks scheme, but we do need some more detail on that. So, will you commit to providing the funding needed to provide 16,000 short breaks for unpaid carers each year for the rest of this Senedd term?

And lastly, I'm just going to turn to mental health. Again, this is an area where I was disappointed not to see a dedicated action from this Plaid Cymru Government for its first 100 days. You've referred today to a fundamental shift in service delivery, but it is unclear what that actually means for people in need of support. So, can the Minister set out today for us what changes will people see in mental health services in Wales this Senedd term, and how many more people will be set to benefit?

contributions.text_english: Newport is at the heart of the world-leading south Wales semiconductor cluster and, over the next four years, the ambition is to grow the cluster revenues to over £1 billion and reach over 6,000 jobs, and this is a huge opportunity to grow local talent. As part of that, companies like KLA and Vishay are engaging with young people and, indeed, parents, because I think parents need to know what some of these jobs are as well: really good quality jobs in a growing sector, right on their doorstep. You've already mentioned the prospective STEM programme with Newport City Council, which is going to be an excellent idea, and I just wonder if you've seen the work that Dragons RFC have done, working with schools and the semiconductor industry, just to really harness that young talent. And what else will the Welsh Government do, working with your Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language, to bring all of this together to make sure we are harnessing that potential of local talent?

contributions.item_title_en: 4. 90-second Statements
contributions.text_english:
Between 1948 and 1971, the UK Government invited people from the Caribbean and Commonwealth countries to help rebuild the country and fill labour shortages after the second world war. On 22 June 1948, HMT Empire Windrush docked in Tilbury. There were 1,027 people on board, mainly from the Caribbean—Jamaica, Saint Lucia, Grenada and Barbados. Many had served in the British armed forces during world war two. The most common sectors that people worked in were the construction industry, public transport, manufacturing and our NHS. In my constituency, we still have Windrush elders. They continue to be important and essential voices in our community. So many have made and continue to make an outstanding contribution.

Vernesta Cyril OBE arrived from Saint Lucia and she is a much-loved midwife in Newport, serving in our NHS for over 40 years. Despite being treated with hostility, Vernesta says it made her strong. She continues to be an inspiration and a leading voice in our community. Roy Grant moved from Jamaica to become an engineer. After arriving in England, he made Newport his home. Roy works relentlessly to make sure young people understand the struggles of the Windrush generation and to help build connections between communities. These are just two people who have made such a positive impact. The elders and their families have made invaluable contributions to Wales. They deserve the respect and gratitude of all of us in this Senedd and across Wales.

contributions.text_english: I'm aware that we need to build more homes of all tenures. The Welsh Labour Government put in record levels of money into social housing, £2 billion in the last Senedd term, which led to record levels of delivery and a healthy pipeline of construction. contributions.text_english: Diolch. From throwing litter out of a car window to the dumping of illegal waste at industrial scales, fly-tipping blights our communities and our environment. contributions.item_title_en: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
contributions.text_english: It's estimated that there are over 20,000 unpaid carers in my constituency, and, last week, I met with the chair of Newport Carers' Forum. The forum are currently focusing on supporting carers with contingency planning. Through no fault of their own, far too many carers have no plans in place for if and when they are unable to provide care. So, these pressures were recognised by the previous Senedd Health and Social Care Committee in their 'At breaking point' report. The report warned that unpaid carers are being pushed to the brink by a system that repeatedly fails to recognise, support or uphold their basic legal rights. Trefnydd, can you commit to the Welsh Government providing a statement in response to the 'At breaking point' report?

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning: Priorities for Local Government, Housing and Planning
contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Mike. Diolch, Deputy Llywydd, and welcome to your role, Cabinet Minister.

Local government is key in making sure front-line services are delivered, and these are services that we rely on day in, day out. The Cabinet Minister says that she wants to renew and strengthen that relationship with local government and the Welsh Government, and I really hope this includes engaging with all local authorities, including those in urban areas, regarding the review of the local government funding formula. The funding formula is based on a complex mix of indicators, and work was ongoing to update some of those indicators. It would be really good to understand whether that work will continue at pace, or whether it will be stopped while there is a review of the funding formula. Also, I know that local authorities would like to know whether the Cabinet Minister expects the funding pot for local authorities to be bigger, or whether the pot will still be the same.

Everyone deserves a place to call home. A warm, secure and affordable home is fundamental to a good life, and the 20,000 new social homes commitment mentioned today is familiar. The Welsh Labour Government invested £2 billion to deliver more than 20,000 homes for rent in the social sector in the last Senedd term. Record levels of delivery combined with record levels of investment helped the sector and the pipeline to be strong. We all know that there was more to do across all tenures, and that's why Welsh Labour committed to deliver 100,000 homes over the next 10 years. The Government has pledged to establish a new national development body and social housing enabler, Unnos. How will the success or failure of Unnos be measured? This is on top of the new-style Welsh Development Agency, and it would be good to know in what way the establishment of quangos cuts bureaucracy and boosts our economy.

The importance of our town centres is something that we should all care about. None of them should be or are the same. I note there was no mention of continuing the Welsh Labour Government's Transforming Towns programme, which boosted regeneration in town and city centres across Wales with more than £300 million since 2020. Also, in terms of the review planned, is it under your responsibility or other Cabinet members' responsibility in terms of having the say over towns more generally, and when will it report?

There was also no mention of the work of the affordable homes taskforce and the implementation group on all those recommendations, which were accepted by Government and by the wider sector. Housing isn’t just about the role of Government. There has to be a team Wales approach to delivering change. So will this Government continue those recommendations?

This Government has, I see, committed to reviewing the Warm Homes programme within the first 100 days in Government. Last year alone, the Welsh Labour Government invested more than £30 million into our enhanced Warm Homes Nest scheme, and we await the detail of the changes this Government will make to the programme, because if there’s no additional funding, we need to know what will be cut.

The Homelessness and Social Housing Allocation (Wales) Act 2026 marked a turning point in how we tackle homelessness here in Wales. The legislation, which I was proud to bring in under the last Welsh Labour Government, gives us a tool to ensure people across Wales access the right support before crisis hits. However, as with any legislation, implementation is key. So, can you, Cabinet Minister, outline how you will ensure that this legislation will actually make a real difference to transform our homelessness system? 

Again, another piece of legislation that went through at the end of the last Senedd term was building safety. I know there's still work to do around the planning and implementation, and I look forward to discussions as that develops. This is absolutely key as part of our response to the Grenfell tragedy. People must feel and be safe in their own homes. 

On your plans on the right to adequate housing—again, this was something that was started in the last Senedd term—Members will be keen to hear what work is to be done ahead of any proposed legislation. I was also glad to see that this Government agrees with the Welsh Labour manifesto commitment to create a community right to buy. Empowering people to keep their special local places for community use is something we should all strive to do, and I know that work on this started under the last Welsh Labour Government. Will this be a year 1 Bill? 

Finally, there was no mention today of support to help get people on the housing ladder. The Welsh Labour Government extended Help to Buy when the Tories closed England's scheme in 2023. How will this Welsh Government help first-time buyers?

On your plans on the right to adequate housing—again, this was something that was started in the last Senedd term—Members will be keen to hear what work is to be done ahead of any proposed legislation. I was also glad to see that this Government agrees with the Welsh Labour manifesto commitment to create a community right to buy. Empowering people to keep their special local places for community use is something we should all strive to do, and I know that work on this started under the last Welsh Labour Government. Will this be a year 1 Bill? 

Finally, there was no mention today of support to help get people on the housing ladder. The Welsh Labour Government extended Help to Buy when the Tories closed England's scheme in 2023. How will this Welsh Government help first-time buyers?

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Transport: Key Infrastructure Resilience
contributions.text_english:
I'd like to welcome the Minister to his position. As a local resident, I know all too well that every time there's an accident or congestion at the Brynglas tunnels, motorway traffic from the M4 is pushed onto our local roads. This creates gridlock, choking the city of Newport and moves air pollution closer to homes and schools.

You said today that you will not repeat the work that has already been done. Are the targeted measures to improve flow and resilience on the existing road network, which you've referred to today, part of the resilience studies for our motorway and trunk roads that were announced by the previous Cabinet Secretary for transport, Ken Skates, last summer? And if this is something different, when will the findings of the reports that were commissioned last year be published? And you ruled out the black route. Will you today rule out the blue route and rule out any closures of junctions?

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the First Minister
contributions.text_english:
As a local resident, I'm very aware of some of the unacceptable delays that people have experienced in accident and emergency at the Grange hospital. I've also been struck by the number of people who have said to me that individual NHS staff members are trying their absolute best to provide excellent care under pressure. The previous Welsh Labour Government invested significantly in the Grange accident and emergency department, because the unacceptably long waits and corridor care experienced by some patients requires action to a systematic level.

An important aspect of improving emergency care is keeping people out of hospital in the first place, as well as the safe and timely discharge of patients to free up capacity in emergency departments. Whether it's working with local authorities on social care, community care, or transfers to other hospitals, like the Royal Gwent, how is the Welsh Government going to fund the integration of pathways out of acute hospital care?

contributions.item_title_en: 4. Business Statement and Announcement
contributions.text_english: Diolch, Lywydd. Trefnydd, as it's Volunteers Week, I'd like to ask for a statement on support for the voluntary sector. There are over 46,000 voluntary organisations in Wales, with one third of the adult population volunteering. And we also know that many young people choose to give up their time to help others. The Wales Council for Voluntary Action have calculated that, last year, voluntary organisations saved the public sector around £1.4 billion, and their total contribution to Wales in 2025 was estimated to be at least £9.1 billion. The Gwent Association of Voluntary Organisations, GAVO, is the largest county voluntary council in Wales, and it's fast approaching 100 years of supporting volunteers in Newport and Islwyn and wider Gwent. As a Co-operative Party member, I was very glad that Welsh Labour pledged to double the number of co-operatives and community-owned businesses, safeguard funding for community cohesion workers, and expand the system of volunteering credits. So, I'd like a statement on how the current Welsh Government plans to support volunteers and voluntary organisations, who are the bedrock of our communities all year round.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care: Health and Care Priorities
contributions.text_english: I welcome the Cabinet Minister to his role. One in three deaths in Gwent between 2018 and 2022 happened prematurely and some of those were preventable. The three main causes were cardiovascular disease, diabetes and cancer. In my constituency, both County in the Community and Dragons Rugby Football Club work extensively with people of all ages, and both men and women. Newport County's Fit Fans programme is a great example of sport taking a leading role in preventative health for both men and women. Grass-roots sports clubs play a leading role as well, and their impact is far-reaching. Sport helps to tackle obesity and prevent other physical and mental health conditions, whilst also tackling loneliness and social isolation. I was surprised that there was no mention of mental health, and also surprised there was no mention of women's health, in the Minister's statement today. But Plaid Cymru's manifesto included a commitment to investing in sports and physical activity as part of the preventative health agenda. Can the Minister tell us how much that investment will be and where the money will come from?
